8:["$","$L13",null,{"data":{"chapterId":2,"verseId":15,"chapterTitle":"Examination of Motion","totalVerses":25,"verseData":{"id":"v2_15","number":15,"title":"Stationarity Is Equally Empty","sanskrit":{"text":"","transliteration":"","translation":"Just as a moving thing is not stationary, A non-moving thing is not stationary. Apart from the moving and the non-moving, What third thing is stationary?"},"philosophy":{"insight":"The analysis now pivots: if motion is empty, is stationarity (rest) inherently real? No. A moving thing can't be inherently stationary. A non-moving thing merely LACKS motion — it doesn't positively POSSESS \"stationarity.\" And no third category exists. Rest is as empty as motion.","madhyamaka":"Garfield: this verse opens the stationarity section (v.15-17), applying the same trilemma to rest. The symmetry is deliberate — emptiness applies equally to motion and its apparent opposite. Kalupahana: \"non-moving\" (agamana) and \"stationary\" (sthiti) are distinguished. Mere absence of motion doesn't equal inherent stationarity. Siderits/Katsura: the verse prevents escape into stationarity as a refuge from the emptiness of motion.","quantum":"Conjugate Variable Uncertainty (Position-Momentum): A particle with perfectly defined position (Δx = 0, truly \"stationary\") has completely undefined momentum (Δp → ∞). Conversely, a particle with defined momentum has undefined position. You cannot have a particle that is both perfectly located AND perfectly still — the two concepts are complementary, not independently fixable.","bridge":"Both show that \"rest\" (stationarity) cannot be an independently established inherent property. In quantum mechanics, perfect stillness (zero momentum) means perfect delocalisation (position undefined). In Madhyamaka, being non-moving doesn't grant inherent stationarity. Both frameworks deny \"rest\" as an independently achievable, inherent state.","accessible":"Is a parked car \"inherently stationary\"? It's on a spinning Earth, orbiting the Sun, hurtling through the galaxy. \"Stationary\" depends on your reference frame — it's not an inherent property. Nāgārjuna makes the same point: nothing is inherently at rest.","twoTruths":"Conventionally, mover and motion are distinguishable. Ultimately, neither can be found independently — they are like two sides of one coin, inseparable under analysis.","commonMisconception":"Not saying mover and motion are 'the same thing.' Saying neither has INDEPENDENT existence — each is constituted by its relation to the other."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"Position-Momentum Uncertainty / Conjugate Variables","score":90,"strength":"High","explanation":"Perfect stationarity (zero momentum) implies infinite position uncertainty — \"rest\" cannot be an inherent, independently fixed state. Direct parallel.","caveat":"Structural analogy illustrating shared patterns between quantum physics and Madhyamaka analysis. Educational metaphor, not literal equivalence."},"animation":{"geometry":"Apparently Still Particle","anchor":"A particle that appears perfectly still — but zoom in and it's jittering (quantum zero-point motion). But absence of motion doesn't positively establish an inherent property called \"stationarity.\" Being non-moving is relational (defined by absence of motion), not an inherent, positive nature.","realLifeExample":"Being \"not hungry\" doesn't mean you're inherently \"full.\" It just means hunger is absent. \"Not hungry\" and \"full\" are different things — one is absence, the other would be an inherent positive state."},{"q":"Why is there no \"third thing\" that is stationary?","a":"Everything is either moving or non-moving (within the essentialist framework). There's no third category. Since neither moving things nor non-moving things are inherently stationary, nothing is. The framework has been exhausted — stationarity finds no home.","realLifeExample":"Every number is either positive, negative, or zero. If none of these categories contains \"inherent bigness,\" then nothing is inherently big. The categories are exhausted."},{"q":"How does position-momentum uncertainty prevent inherent rest?","a":"The uncertainty principle ΔxΔp ≥ ħ/2 means: if a particle has perfectly defined position (truly \"located\" somewhere, Δx → 0), its momentum becomes completely uncertain (Δp → ∞). It could be moving at any speed in any direction! \"Perfectly located\" doesn't mean \"perfectly still\" — it means wildly uncertain motion.","realLifeExample":"Trapping a cat in a tiny box (fixing its position precisely) makes it bounce off the walls more violently (momentum uncertainty increases). The more you \"fix\" its location, the less \"still\" it becomes."},{"q":"What about zero-point energy?","a":"Even at absolute zero temperature, quantum systems retain zero-point energy — they never truly stop moving. The ground state of a harmonic oscillator has energy ½ħω, not zero. Quantum mechanics literally prevents perfect stationarity.","realLifeExample":"Liquid helium never freezes at normal pressure, no matter how cold it gets — zero-point motion keeps it liquid. Nature itself prevents perfect stillness."},{"q":"Why does Nāgārjuna analyse stationarity after motion?","a":"To prevent the escape route: \"Okay, motion is empty, but REST is real!\" Nāgārjuna shows the opposite of motion is equally empty. Neither motion nor rest has inherent existence. Both are conventional designations, not ultimate realities.","realLifeExample":"If someone proves \"hot\" has no inherent meaning, you might retreat to \"Well, cold is real!\" But cold is just the absence of heat — equally empty of inherent nature. Neither extreme is independently real."},{"q":"How does this verse connect to v.16-17?","a":"V.15 shows stationarity is unfindable in moving, non-moving, or third categories. V.16 shows the contradiction of a moving thing being stationary. V.17 shows transitions (starting, stopping) are equally analysable — and equally empty. The stationarity section mirrors the motion section in structure and conclusion.","deeper":"The v.15-17 block is deliberately parallel to v.1-3.
